logan.intro: Logan sits in the Hocking Hills, and the oldest thing in the town grows on the northeast corner of its old cemetery. The Great White Oak has stood there for roughly six centuries, its limbs leaving the trunk sideways rather than upward. The town has organised itself around keeping it going: the Tree Commission gathers the acorns, raises them into saplings and sells them as a fundraiser, so there are young oaks all over Hocking County with this one as the parent.
logan.meta_description: Logan's great white oak has stood in the old cemetery for about 600 years, and the town raises seedlings from its acorns.
logan.question_answer: The oldest tree in Logan is the Great White Oak, a white oak of roughly 600 years on the northeast corner of Old Logan Cemetery, near the junction of Keynes Drive and North Mulberry Street. The Ohio Department of Natural Resources checked its age about thirty years ago, but the method was never recorded, so the honest range is 500 to 650 years. It is free, on public cemetery ground, and easy to pick out: it is the largest thing standing there by a wide margin.
logan.question_meta: The Great White Oak in Old Logan Cemetery is Logan's oldest tree, roughly 600 years old and free to visit on public ground.
logan.question_context:
Logan is in Hocking County, about an hour southeast of Columbus, and no public transport reaches the tree. You drive, and you park at Old Logan Cemetery on the north side of town. The oak is on the northeast corner, near where Keynes Drive meets North Mulberry Street. The cemetery is public ground with no gate and no charge, and visitors who behave as one behaves in a cemetery are welcome.

What is there is one white oak, not a collection. An Ohio naturalist spent an hour photographing it in 2019 and called it easily the largest and most ornate white oak he had seen, which is the fair description: huge gnarled limbs going out sideways, the frame an oak only builds with room and several centuries.

Autumn is the moment to plan for. The acorns drop in September and October and the Tree Commission collects them, grows them on and sells the saplings. Nobody appears to have put a tape around the trunk. If you have, we would like the number.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree in Logan?
faq.a: The Great White Oak on the northeast corner of Old Logan Cemetery, put at roughly 600 years. The state's natural resources department checked the age about thirty years ago without recording the method, so 500 to 650 years is the range worth quoting.

faq.q: Is the Logan Oak free to visit?
faq.a: Yes. It stands on the grounds of Old Logan Cemetery, which is public, has no gate and charges nothing. It is a cemetery, so the usual quiet applies.

faq.q: How do I get to the Logan Oak?
faq.a: By car. Logan is about an hour southeast of Columbus in Hocking County, and there is no public transport to the tree. Head for Old Logan Cemetery and the junction of Keynes Drive and North Mulberry Street; the oak is on the northeast corner.

faq.q: When is the best time to see it?
faq.a: September and October, when the acorns drop. The Logan Tree Commission collects them, raises the seedlings and sells them to fund more planting, so autumn is also when the tree is visibly doing something for the town.

martinsville.intro: One oak stands alone in an open field off Mountain Road, and New Jersey has been telling stories about it for decades. The Devil's Tree is the state's best known haunted landmark: cars that will not start, a trunk said to stay warm, scratches nobody gave. What is verifiably true is harder than the folklore. People have attacked it with axes and chainsaws for years and failed, and the scars are still on the trunk, which is now ringed by a fence.
martinsville.meta_description: New Jersey's Devil's Tree stands alone in a Martinsville field, scarred by decades of axes and chainsaws and fenced off after the vandalism.
martinsville.question_answer: The oldest tree in Martinsville is the Devil's Tree, an oak of at least 200 years standing by itself in an open field off Mountain Road, in the Martinsville section of Bernards Township. No botanical survey has established which oak it is, so it is listed here as Quercus, and 200 years is a floor rather than a measurement. The field is public open space and free to enter, but a chain-link fence around the trunk keeps visitors at a few paces.
martinsville.question_meta: Martinsville's Devil's Tree is an oak of at least 200 years, alone in a public field off Mountain Road, fenced and free to visit by day.
martinsville.question_context:
Martinsville is part of Bernards Township in Somerset County, and there is no public transport to the tree. It is a car trip, off Mountain Road, and the field it stands in is undeveloped land the township designated as public open space. A sign posted in 2007 gives the hours, closing about half an hour after sunset, which is aimed squarely at the night visits that made the fence necessary.

Expect one tree in an empty field, and expect to look at it rather than touch it. The chain-link ring went up after years of vandalism, including attempts to burn and to fell it, and the axe and chainsaw scars are visible from outside the fence.

One thing to get straight before you drive: this is not the Basking Ridge oak. That was a different tree, a 600 year old white oak a few miles away, which died in 2016 and was removed the following year. It is regularly confused with this one. The Devil's Tree is alive.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree in Martinsville?
faq.a: The Devil's Tree, an oak of at least 200 years standing alone in a field off Mountain Road. Nobody has dated it precisely and no survey has established which species of oak it is, so both figures are open questions.

faq.q: Can you get close to the Devil's Tree?
faq.a: Close, but not up to it. The field is public open space you can walk into freely; the trunk itself is enclosed by a chain-link fence installed after years of vandalism, so it is a look rather than a touch.

faq.q: Is the Devil's Tree really haunted?
faq.a: The stories are genuine folklore and widely retold: a car that refuses to start, a trunk warm in cold weather, scratches appearing on visitors. None of it has ever been demonstrated. The scarring on the trunk, from decades of people trying to cut and burn the tree down, is the part that is documented.

faq.q: Is this the Basking Ridge oak?
faq.a: No, and the two get mixed up constantly. The Basking Ridge white oak was about 600 years old, stood a few miles away, died in 2016 and was taken down in 2017. The Devil's Tree is a different tree and is still standing.

oklahoma-city.intro: The tree on this page stood in a car park across the street from the Alfred P. Murrah Federal Building. On 19 April 1995 the bombing stripped away most of its branches and drove glass and debris into its trunk, and investigators nearly took it down to recover that debris as evidence. It was left standing, and about a year later it came into bloom again. It is now the centre of the outdoor grounds of the Oklahoma City National Memorial.
oklahoma-city.meta_description: The Survivor Tree came through the 1995 Oklahoma City bombing and bloomed again the next spring. It stands at the National Memorial, free, all hours.
oklahoma-city.question_answer: Oklahoma City's most significant old tree is the Survivor Tree, an American elm of around 100 years standing at the Outdoor Symbolic Memorial of the Oklahoma City National Memorial, 620 N Harvey Avenue. Photographs of the site from the 1920s, when the ground was the back yard of a family home, show it already growing. Older trees very likely stand elsewhere in the city; none of them is recorded, and none of them is this one.
oklahoma-city.question_meta: The Survivor Tree, an American elm of about 100 years, stands at the Oklahoma City National Memorial. Free, open every hour of the year.
oklahoma-city.question_context:
The tree stands on the north side of the Oklahoma City National Memorial at 620 N Harvey Avenue, downtown, above the Field of Empty Chairs and within the Gates of Time. The Outdoor Symbolic Memorial, which is where the tree is, is open 24 hours a day, 365 days a year and costs nothing. Only the separate indoor museum charges admission, and you do not need it to see the elm.

What you find is one tree in a place built around it. The Rescuers' Orchard, planted with redbuds, maples and elms, stands around it, and seed is collected from the elm each year and grown on, with seedlings going to visitors and to partner sites elsewhere in the country.

It is a working memorial rather than a park, and people come to it for reasons that have nothing to do with trees. Visit it as you would any memorial: quietly, and at your own pace. There is no charge, no ticket and no closing time.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree in Oklahoma City?
faq.a: The Survivor Tree, the American elm at the Oklahoma City National Memorial, is the oldest tree in the city with a documented history. Photographs from the 1920s show it already growing on what was then a private back yard, which puts it at around 100 years.

faq.q: Is it free to see the Survivor Tree?
faq.a: Yes. The Outdoor Symbolic Memorial is open every hour of every day of the year at no charge. The indoor museum on the same site charges admission, but the tree is not inside it.

faq.q: Where exactly is the Survivor Tree?
faq.a: On the north side of the memorial grounds at 620 N Harvey Avenue in downtown Oklahoma City, on a raised terrace above the Field of Empty Chairs, with the Rescuers' Orchard planted around it.

faq.q: What happened to the tree in the bombing?
faq.a: The blast stripped most of its branches and embedded glass and debris in the trunk. Investigators considered felling it to recover that material as evidence. It was left in place, bloomed again roughly a year later, and was made the centrepiece of the memorial.

olympic-national-park.intro: Olympic National Park runs to nearly a million acres, and this is one tree inside it, a few hundred feet off Highway 101 between Ruby Beach and Kalaloch. The Kalaloch cedar was once counted among the largest western red cedars anywhere. In March 2014 a coastal storm split it down its length and roughly half of it came down. The other half is still standing and still alive, which makes it a stranger and more interesting stop than the record-holder was.
olympic-national-park.meta_description: A storm split the Kalaloch cedar in two in 2014. Half of this thousand-year-old western red cedar still stands, a few feet off Highway 101.
olympic-national-park.question_answer: Olympic National Park holds trees nobody has ever dated, but the oldest one with a name, a trail and a sign is the Kalaloch cedar, a western red cedar of roughly a thousand years, off Highway 101 between Ruby Beach and Kalaloch. Estimates for it run from 800 to 1,200 years. Half of it came down in a storm in March 2014; the standing half is alive, in slow decline, and reached by a flat trail of a few hundred feet from a signed roadside pull-off.
olympic-national-park.question_meta: The Kalaloch cedar, roughly 1,000 years old, is the named old tree of Olympic National Park's coast strip. Free, just off Highway 101.
olympic-national-park.question_context:
Olympic National Park comes in three parts: mountains, rainforest and a long coastal strip. This tree is on the coastal strip, on Highway 101 between Ruby Beach and Kalaloch, and reaching it costs nothing. The Big Cedar trail leaves a signed roadside pull-off and runs a few hundred feet, flat, to the tree. The access road has potholes and is passable in any car. The nearest services are at Kalaloch Lodge a few miles south, and there is no public transport on this coast.

Go knowing what is there. The dimensions this cedar is famous for, close to six metres through and about fifty three metres tall, date from before March 2014, when a coastal storm split the trunk and brought down roughly half of it. Nobody has published a remeasurement since. What stands now is a great damaged column, alive but declining, with the fallen half beside it. The signs at the tree cover the damage and where it is sensible to stand, and they are current guidance rather than history.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree in Olympic National Park?
faq.a: Plenty of trees in the park have never been dated, so the honest answer is the oldest one that is named and signed: the Kalaloch cedar, a western red cedar estimated at 800 to 1,200 years, on the coast strip off Highway 101.

faq.q: Do I need to pay to see the Kalaloch cedar?
faq.a: No. The Big Cedar trail runs a few hundred feet off a roadside pull-off on Highway 101, with no entrance station between the road and the tree.

faq.q: Is the tree still alive after the 2014 storm?
faq.a: Yes. The March 2014 storm split it and took down roughly half the trunk and crown. The remaining half is alive and has been described since as in slow decline. Trip reports treat it as a standing, visitable tree.

faq.q: How long is the walk?
faq.a: A few hundred feet, flat and well marked, from the signed parking pull-off. It is one of the shortest walks to a tree of this age anywhere on the Washington coast.

palo-alto.intro: Palo Alto is named after a tree, and the tree is still there, on the bank of San Francisquito Creek with Caltrain going past a few metres away. El Palo Alto is a coast redwood of about a thousand years, and its name means the tall stick, which has become slightly awkward: it has lost roughly sixteen metres off the top since 1930, as the water table under the creek was drawn down. The city and local arborists have spent real money keeping it alive.
palo-alto.meta_description: El Palo Alto, the thousand-year-old redwood the city is named after, has lost 16 metres off its top since 1930 and is still standing.
palo-alto.question_answer: The oldest tree in Palo Alto is El Palo Alto, the coast redwood the city takes its name from, estimated at about a thousand years and by some accounts a little over eleven hundred. It stands in El Palo Alto Park on the bank of San Francisquito Creek by Alma Street, next to the Caltrain tracks, free and reachable at any hour. It appears on the city seal, and a Spanish expedition is recorded camping at this creek in 1769.
palo-alto.question_meta: El Palo Alto, a coast redwood of about 1,000 years, is Palo Alto's oldest tree and its namesake. Free, on the creek bank by Alma Street.
palo-alto.question_context:
El Palo Alto Park is a small strip on the bank of San Francisquito Creek by Alma Street, where the Caltrain corridor crosses it. It is walkable from downtown Palo Alto and from the University Avenue station, free, open, and reachable at any hour. There is one tree here that anybody comes for.

It is not the largest redwood you will ever see, and that is the story rather than a disappointment. It measured 162 feet in 1930 and stands at about 110 today, roughly thirty three and a half metres, with a dead top, because the water table beneath the creek was drawn down between 1865 and 1955 and the crown died back as the water went.

What is unusual is how closely it is now watched. A donated assessment in March 2025 ran ground-penetrating radar beneath it, excavated the roots with compressed air, flew a drone through the crown and left a prism on the trunk to measure movement. The finding was decay and a dead top on sound buttress roots.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree in Palo Alto?
faq.a: El Palo Alto, the coast redwood on San Francisquito Creek that the city is named after. Estimates put it at about a thousand years, and some at a little over eleven hundred.

faq.q: How do I get to El Palo Alto?
faq.a: It is in El Palo Alto Park on the creek bank by Alma Street, beside the railway. Walkable from downtown Palo Alto and from the University Avenue Caltrain station. The park is free and open.

faq.q: Why is the tree shorter than it used to be?
faq.a: The water table under San Francisquito Creek was drawn down between 1865 and 1955, and the crown died back progressively as the water went. It measured 162 feet in 1930 and stands at about 110 feet now, with a dead top.

faq.q: Is El Palo Alto still healthy?
faq.a: It is alive and actively monitored. An assessment in March 2025 using ground-penetrating radar, root excavation and drone survey found decay and a dead top, but sound buttress roots. A prism on the trunk tracks whether the tree moves.

sequoia-national-park.intro: General Sherman is not the tallest tree, and it is probably not the oldest in its own grove. It is the largest known living single-stem tree on Earth by volume, about 1,487 cubic metres of trunk, and it stands on the Main Trail in the Giant Forest, half a mile from the parking lot that carries its name. In September 2021, with the KNP Complex Fire burning into the grove, park staff wrapped its base in aluminium foil. It worked.
sequoia-national-park.meta_description: General Sherman holds 1,487 cubic metres of trunk, the largest living tree on Earth. Staff wrapped its base in foil to save it from fire in 2021.
sequoia-national-park.question_answer: General Sherman is the giant sequoia at the centre of the Giant Forest in Sequoia National Park, most often dated at 2,300 to 2,700 years, with older estimates running as high as 3,200. It is the largest living single-stem tree on Earth by volume rather than the oldest: other sequoias in the same grove may well be older, and none has been cored to settle it. It is a half-mile walk from the Sherman Tree parking lot, downhill on the way in.
sequoia-national-park.question_meta: General Sherman, 2,300 to 2,700 years old, stands in the Giant Forest in Sequoia National Park, half a mile from the parking lot.
sequoia-national-park.question_context:
Sequoia National Park is large, and General Sherman is the reason most first-time visitors drive into this part of it. The tree stands in the Giant Forest, on the Main Trail, about half a mile from the Sherman Tree parking lot. The walk in is downhill and partly paved, which makes the walk out the uphill one. A seasonal shuttle runs for anyone who would rather not do it twice.

The park charges an entrance fee at the gate. Once you are through, the tree costs nothing. There is no public transport into the park, and the nearest town is Three Rivers, about 45 minutes' drive from the entrance.

The thing worth knowing before you arrive is that the fame is about bulk, not height. At 83.6 metres it is an ordinary tall sequoia. At about 31 metres round the base it is not, and the roughly 1,487 cubic metres of trunk is what makes it the largest living single-stem tree on the planet.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree in Sequoia National Park?
faq.a: Nobody knows, and General Sherman is not a safe answer to that question. It is dated at 2,300 to 2,700 years, with older estimates as high as 3,200, but other sequoias in the Giant Forest may be older and none of them has been cored. What General Sherman holds is the volume record.

faq.q: How much does it cost to see General Sherman?
faq.a: Sequoia National Park charges an entrance fee per vehicle at the gate. Beyond that there is nothing to pay: the trail to the tree is open and free once you are inside the park.

faq.q: How long is the walk to General Sherman?
faq.a: About half a mile each way from the Sherman Tree parking lot, partly paved. It goes downhill on the way in and uphill on the way back, and a seasonal shuttle covers the route for anyone who wants to skip the climb.

faq.q: Did General Sherman survive the wildfires?
faq.a: Yes. The KNP Complex Fire reached the Giant Forest in September 2021 and park staff wrapped the base of the tree in protective aluminium foil. The tree came through unharmed and was remeasured in 2024.

simsbury.intro: Simsbury built a park around one tree and then put floodlights on it. The Pinchot Sycamore is the largest tree in Connecticut, about thirty metres tall with an average crown spread of forty three, which makes it considerably wider than it is high. It stands on the flood plain of the Farmington River, the wet ground an American sycamore wants, and it carries the name of Gifford Pinchot, the conservationist who later governed the state.
simsbury.meta_description: Connecticut's largest tree stands in its own park in Simsbury: the Pinchot Sycamore, 8.8 metres round, wider than it is tall, floodlit at night.
simsbury.question_answer: Simsbury's oldest known tree is the Pinchot Sycamore, an American sycamore on the east bank of the Farmington River off Route 185, estimated at over 200 years and possibly beyond 300. It is also the largest tree in Connecticut, measured in November 2025 at 884 centimetres round, 30.2 metres tall, with an average crown spread of 43 metres. It stands in its own free public park with a boat launch onto the river, and has been floodlit at night since 1997.
simsbury.question_meta: The Pinchot Sycamore, over 200 years old and Connecticut's largest tree, stands in a free park on the Farmington River in Simsbury.
simsbury.question_context:
Pinchot Sycamore Park is on the east bank of the Farmington River on Route 185, south of Simsbury's village centre and below Talcott Mountain. There is no direct public transport, so it is a car trip. The park is free and open, and the tree is the whole reason for it: open lawn, a boat launch onto the river, and floodlights that have been on the tree since 1997.

It was measured most recently in November 2025 at 884 centimetres round, 30.2 metres tall, with an average spread of 43 metres, which is what makes it Connecticut's largest tree and the national champion of its species. The age is given as over 200 years and possibly past 300. There is no planting date and it has never been cored.

Winter is the moment worth choosing. A sycamore this size is at its most legible with the leaves off, when the white upper limbs and the whole frame of the crown show, and the floodlights make the same case after dark.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree in Simsbury?
faq.a: The Pinchot Sycamore, on the Farmington River off Route 185. It is estimated at over 200 years and possibly beyond 300, with no planting date on record.

faq.q: Is the Pinchot Sycamore really the largest tree in Connecticut?
faq.a: Yes, on the state's own notable-trees record, and it is listed as the national champion for its species. Its last measurement, in November 2025, gave 884 centimetres of circumference, a height of 30.2 metres and an average crown spread of 43 metres.

faq.q: Is it free to visit, and how do I get there?
faq.a: Free, in a public town park with open grounds and a boat launch. It is on Route 185 south of Simsbury centre and there is no direct public transport, so you will need a car.

faq.q: When is the best time to see it?
faq.a: January and February. With the leaves off, the white upper limbs and the full frame of the crown are visible, which is the thing this tree is actually remarkable for. The floodlights have been on it since 1997, so it also reads after dark.

sunderland.intro: Sunderland's buttonball tree was already large when the United States Constitution was signed, and the plaque at its foot dates it that way. It stands on the verge of North Main Street in the middle of the village: 782 centimetres round, over thirty four metres tall, with a crown spreading about forty three metres, and it is widely called the largest tree in Massachusetts. Tradition puts its seeding before 1665, which makes it well over three hundred and fifty years old.
sunderland.meta_description: Sunderland's Buttonball Tree was already large when the Constitution was signed in 1787. It stands free on North Main Street, roadside.
sunderland.question_answer: The oldest tree in Sunderland is the Buttonball Tree, an American sycamore on North Main Street in the town centre. Tradition holds that it seeded before 1665, which puts it well over 350 years old and by some accounts close to 400. It measured 782 centimetres round at chest height in 2019, over 34 metres tall, with a crown spreading about 43 metres, and it is widely called the largest tree in Massachusetts. It stands on a public verge, free, with a plaque installed beside it in 1987.
sunderland.question_meta: Sunderland's Buttonball Tree, an American sycamore of over 350 years, stands free on North Main Street and is called Massachusetts' largest tree.
sunderland.question_context:
Sunderland is in the Connecticut River valley in western Massachusetts, roughly 25 minutes north of Amherst by road, and there is no public transport to the tree. It stands on the verge of North Main Street in the middle of the village, so there is no park to enter and no gate: you park, walk over and put a hand on the bark. A commemorative plaque went in beside it in 1987.

The measurements date from November 2019: 782 centimetres round at chest height, over 34 metres tall, an average spread of 43 metres. An arbor column revisited the tree in April 2026 and readers reported the girth has grown since, which is a good sign rather than a figure to quote.

The age is tradition rather than a count of rings. The town holds that the tree seeded before 1665, and the stone plaque makes the point by dating it against the signing of the Constitution in 1787, by which time it was already large. The local claim goes further, that it is the widest tree this side of the Mississippi.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree in Sunderland?
faq.a: The Buttonball Tree on North Main Street. Tradition dates its seeding to before 1665, making it well over 350 years old and by some accounts close to 400. Nobody has cored it, so that is tradition rather than a measurement.

faq.q: Is the Buttonball Tree the largest tree in Massachusetts?
faq.a: It is widely described as such, on a girth of 782 centimetres measured in 2019 and a crown spread of about 43 metres. The stronger local claim, that it is the widest tree this side of the Mississippi, is a saying rather than a survey.

faq.q: Is it free to visit, and where exactly is it?
faq.a: Free, and there is nothing to enter. It stands roadside on the verge of North Main Street in Sunderland town centre, with the 1987 plaque in front of it. You will need a car; there is no public transport.

faq.q: Why is it called a buttonball tree?
faq.a: Buttonball is the New England name for the American sycamore, after the round seed balls that hang on the bare limbs through winter before breaking apart in spring. December and January are when they are most visible.

tillamook.intro: Twenty minutes west of Tillamook, on the headland at Cape Meares, stands a Sitka spruce with no trunk. Six heavy limbs leave a base about fifteen metres wide, run out sideways as far as five metres and only then turn and climb. It is called the Octopus Tree, and also the Candelabra Tree, the Council Tree and, by someone less taken with it, the Monstrosity Tree. Local tradition says Native people shaped it deliberately. That account is disputed.
tillamook.meta_description: The Octopus Tree at Cape Meares has no trunk: six limbs run sideways from a 15-metre base before turning up. Free, minutes from Tillamook.
tillamook.question_answer: The oldest tree at Tillamook is the Octopus Tree, a Sitka spruce of roughly 250 to 300 years at the Cape Meares State Scenic Viewpoint, a few minutes' walk from the lighthouse parking area about 20 minutes west of the town. It has no central trunk: six large limbs splay horizontally from a base roughly fifteen metres wide before turning vertical, and the base measures over fourteen metres round. Oregon lists it as a Heritage Tree, and it is free to visit.
tillamook.question_meta: The Octopus Tree, a 250 to 300 year old Sitka spruce with no trunk, stands free at Cape Meares, 20 minutes west of Tillamook.
tillamook.question_context:
Cape Meares State Scenic Viewpoint is on the headland about 20 to 25 minutes' drive west of Tillamook, and there is no public transport to it. Park at the Cape Meares Lighthouse parking area; the tree is a short, easy, well-marked walk from there, and none of it costs anything.

The form is the reason to come. There is no central trunk. Six large limbs leave a base roughly fifteen metres across, run out horizontally for as much as five metres and then turn upward, which is how the tree collected its four names. The circumference at the base is over fourteen metres and the age is put at roughly 250 to 300 years.

How it grew this way is unsettled. Local tradition holds that Native people trained the young spruce, and one version of that story says the limbs were meant to cradle canoes in burial rites. The account is debated and has never been confirmed. Oregon lists the tree as a Heritage Tree, which is a designation rather than an explanation.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree in Tillamook?
faq.a: The Octopus Tree at Cape Meares, a Sitka spruce of roughly 250 to 300 years, about 20 minutes' drive west of the town.

faq.q: Why does the Octopus Tree have no trunk?
faq.a: Nobody has settled it. Local tradition says Native people trained the young spruce into shape, in one version to cradle canoes in burial rites, and that account is disputed and unconfirmed. What is certain is the result: six limbs running horizontally from a base about fifteen metres wide before turning vertical.

faq.q: Is it free, and how do I get there?
faq.a: Free. It is in the Cape Meares State Scenic Viewpoint, a short and easy signed walk from the lighthouse parking area. There is no public transport, so it is a 20 to 25 minute drive west from Tillamook.

faq.q: What else is the tree called?
faq.a: The Candelabra Tree, the Council Tree and the Monstrosity Tree, all for the same reason. It is also a designated Oregon Heritage Tree.
